strengths: Novel graph prior design combining multiple SBMs and preferential attachment that thoughtfully addresses limitations of single SBM approaches
Solid experimental methodology with 10 runs, multiple datasets spanning diverse domains, and comprehensive baseline comparisons
Strong finetuning results on accessible datasets (7 of 10 show best performance, with substantial improvements on several datasets like artnet-exp and hm-prices)
Demonstrates importance of pretraining via Table 4 comparison with random graph adapters, validating the pretraining contribution
Honest and comprehensive limitations discussion, acknowledging scalability constraints, domain coverage gaps, and task restrictions
Reasonable architectural design choices that reduce computational overhead (e.g., initializing from pretrained LimiX, freezing backbone layers)
weaknesses: Severe scalability limitations prevent evaluation on 31% of datasets (4 of 13 fail with OOM during finetuning), undermining state-of-the-art claims where method cannot run on some benchmark datasets

Inconsistent and often weak in-context learning performance with substantial gaps on some datasets (hm-prices: -6.94%, city-roads-M: -5.6% vs G2T-LimiX), suggesting poor prior coverage of certain real-world graph types

Insufficient validation of graph prior quality—no quantitative comparison of structural properties (degree distributions, clustering, motifs) between synthetic and real graphs despite this being central to PFN framework

Limited experimental analysis with missing ablations on critical design choices (MGM loss weight=0.1, attribute mixing probability p, importance of each SBM component) and no analysis of learned attention patterns
Incomplete comparisons with concurrent work (TabGFM mentioned but not evaluated) and missing important baselines from related work
Modest novelty in core components—graph adapters are straightforward message-passing extensions; main contribution is graph prior design which is incremental over existing techniques

strengths: First PFN-based model genuinely pretrained on synthetic graph data with graph-aware objectives (supervised + masked graph modeling), advancing beyond hand-crafted feature approaches like G2T-FM and TAG
Thoughtfully designed graph prior combining multi-level SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCMs; well-validated in Appendix B with numerical analysis and ablations on simpler alternatives
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 13 diverse datasets, 10 runs with std, both ICL and finetuning settings, multiple baseline comparisons, and good ablations (e.g., Table 5-6, Figure 2)
Strong empirical results: achieves best performance on 10/13 datasets when finetuned with ensembling, often by substantial margins (≥1 percentage point on multiple datasets)
Honest discussion of limitations in Appendix A (scalability, prior domain coverage, class restrictions, task scope) and clear reproducibility (training details, code promised, ablations provided)
Clear presentation with helpful figures (especially Figure 1 architecture diagram) and comprehensive appendix with graph characteristic analysis and visualization
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: graph adapters are standard scaled dot-product attention masked by adjacency matrix. Main novelty resides in the graph prior design, not the architecture itself

Restricted experimental scope: limited to small-medium graphs (largest ~170K nodes) and ≤10 classes; excludes >10 class problems due to TFM limitations. This significantly constrains claims about practical utility on modern graph benchmarks

Ad-hoc design choices with insufficient justification: MGM loss weight (0.1) not ablated; freezing LimiX layers except adapters not compared to unfrozen alternatives; GNN neuron mixing probability discretization and multi-level SBM construction both appear unmotivated

Statistical significance concerns: Many ICL improvements are small (1-2 percentage points, often within error bars). Ensembling provides large gains, but makes single-model comparisons harder to interpret. Some baseline results missing (TAG on GraphLand datasets)

Incremental contribution over prior work: primary differences from G2T-FM are adding message-passing adapters and using graph prior instead of hand-crafted features. While useful, this represents contained advancement rather than fundamental innovation

Scalability not addressed: acknowledged limitation that entire dataset must be processed at once leads to significant memory consumption. No exploration of sampling-based or memory-efficient alternatives discussed

Incomplete ablation studies: missing comparisons on supervised vs. MGM loss weighting; unclear how much improvement comes from pretraining vs. architecture vs. ensembling; random adapter ablation (Table 6) helps but is limited in scope

Graph prior coverage concerns: synthetic statistics show high variance in some dimensions (e.g., average degree 2.39-479 vs. real 3.75-460), and prior is acknowledged to not cover specific domains like traffic networks
